title: Failed Window Seals & Flashing: Slow Water Intrusion | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: Why window seals and flashing fail, how slow leaks hide inside walls, and what the stains, bubbling paint and soft drywall under a window are telling you.
h1: Failed Window Seals & Flashing as a Slow Water Intrusion Path
intro: You have painted that corner under the window twice now. Maybe three times. The paint went on fine, looked right for a season, and then the same faint brown edge came back, a little wider than before. Nobody in the house did anything to cause it. It does not happen every week, so it is hard to point at a cause, and it is easy to talk yourself out of worrying about it. But you keep noticing it. There is a specific kind of tiredness that comes from a problem that will not declare itself, that shows up just often enough to stay in your head and never clearly enough to fix. If you have been quietly wondering for months why this keeps coming back, that instinct is worth taking seriously, and it deserves to be understood before anyone tells you what to do about it.

sections.heading: A window is not one seal, it is several, and they fail at different speeds
sections.body:
Most people picture a window leak as water running through the glass or around the frame in an obvious stream. That is rarely what is happening. A window assembly relies on a stack of separate barriers, and any one of them can quit while the others look fine.

The insulated glass unit seal is the black or grey spacer bond between the two panes. When it fails you get fogging, haze, or mineral streaking between the panes that you cannot wipe off. That one is usually a comfort and clarity problem, not a wall problem.

The perimeter caulk joint where the frame meets stucco or siding is the barrier most people see. Sun, heat cycling and movement pull it away from one side of the joint, often at the top corners first, and a hairline separation you cannot see from the ground is enough.

The flashing is the part almost nobody sees, and it is the one that matters most. Flashing is the sheet metal, self adhered membrane, or pan under and around the window opening that is supposed to catch anything that gets past the caulk and route it back out to the surface of the wall. If flashing was installed backwards, lapped the wrong direction, cut short at the corners, or simply left out and replaced with a bead of sealant, then the caulk is the only thing standing between your wall cavity and the weather. When that caulk ages, water has a direct path into the framing, and gravity takes it from there.

The weep system is the small slots along the bottom of a vinyl or aluminum frame. Windows are designed to let a little water in and drain it back out. Painted over, caulked shut, or packed with dust and stucco slurry, those weeps stop draining and the sill track becomes a shallow reservoir that eventually finds the interior.

sections.eyebrow: Why it takes so long to notice
sections.heading: Slow intrusion hides its own evidence, especially in a dry climate
sections.body:
A slow leak behaves nothing like a burst supply line. The volume is small, it arrives only during specific conditions, and between those events the assembly dries partway out. That drying is what keeps you guessing.

In the Phoenix area the pattern is often seasonal rather than steady. Long stretches of intense sun and heat do the damage: UV breaks down sealant, and the daily expansion and contraction of stucco, frame and glass works joints open a fraction at a time. Then monsoon storms deliver wind driven rain, sideways, against a wall that normally never gets wet, for twenty minutes. A wall that sheds vertical rain fine will take water at that angle. Weeks of nothing, then one storm, then weeks of nothing. That is why the stain seems to move on its own schedule and why the timing never quite lines up with anything you can name.

Irrigation is the other quiet contributor. A spray head that has drifted or a drip line that hits the base of a wall puts water on stucco every single day. It does not need wind. It just needs time.

What makes the delay dangerous is where the water goes. It enters at the head or jamb, runs down inside the wall cavity behind the drywall, and wets the bottom plate, the sill framing, the sheathing and the insulation long before it reaches a surface you can see. Insulation holds it. Drywall wicks it upward. By the time a stain appears on the interior, the wet area behind it is usually taller and wider than the mark on the wall, and the framing has been going through repeated wet and dry cycles for a while.

Microbial growth does not need standing water, only sustained moisture and organic material, which paper faced drywall and wood framing both provide. Growth inside a closed cavity is often smelled before it is seen: a flat, earthy, slightly sour odor near that window on humid mornings or when the room has been closed up.

sections.eyebrow: How to read your own wall
sections.heading: Signs to look for, and a few checks you can do yourself
sections.body:
None of this requires opening a wall. Do it on a calm day, with good light, and take photos so you can compare in a month.

Inside, at the window: run your hand along the bottom of the drywall return and the wall directly below the sill. Look for paint that is bubbled, crazed, or slightly chalky. Press gently with a thumb. Sound drywall is firm. Drywall that has been repeatedly wet feels spongy or gives a little. Check whether the corner bead has a rust colored line bleeding through the paint, which is steel corner bead reacting to moisture behind it. Look at the baseboard below the window for a swollen bottom edge or paint lifting off the top edge.

Check the sill track. Open the window and look at the slots at the outer edge of the track. Are they painted over or filled? Pour a cup of water into the track and see whether it drains outside within a minute or sits there.

Inside the glass: fogging, a hazy film, or a fine white mineral line between the panes means that specific glass unit has lost its seal. Note it, but do not assume it explains a wet wall. Those are two different failures.

Outside, from a ladder or with binoculars: look at the caulk joint at the top corners of the window, where the frame meets the wall. You are looking for a crack you can slide a fingernail into, a joint that has pulled loose from one side, or old caulk that has gone hard and shrunken. Look at the stucco directly above the window for cracks running out from the corners, which is a very common entry point. Look for staining, efflorescence (a white powdery mineral bloom), or a persistently darker patch of stucco below the window that dries slower than the wall around it.

Also look up. Water that shows at a window is not always coming from that window. Failed flashing at a roof to wall intersection, a scupper, a parapet cap, or an upper story window can dump into the cavity and surface at the first horizontal interruption below, which is usually a window head. That is why chasing the stain alone can send you to the wrong place.

One useful test: on a hot afternoon, have someone run a garden hose at low pressure on the wall a couple of feet above the window for ten minutes while you watch the interior, then move to the head, then the jambs, one area at a time. Isolating zones is the whole point. Soaking everything at once tells you there is a leak but not where.

sections.heading: Sealing the surface is usually not the repair, it is the postponement
sections.body: The reason this keeps recurring for so many homeowners is that the visible fix and the actual fix are different jobs. Re-caulking a perimeter joint takes an hour and it can genuinely stop a leak when the caulk was the only thing that failed. But if the flashing behind the frame is missing, reversed, or terminated short at a corner, fresh caulk buys a season or two and then you are repainting that corner again. A real repair follows the water. That means confirming the entry point rather than guessing, then correcting the drainage path so that water which gets past the surface has somewhere to go besides your framing. Depending on what is found, that can mean removing a section of stucco or siding around the opening, installing proper head flashing and a sill pan with end dams, lapping the weather resistive barrier over the flashing in the correct shingle order, and only then re-finishing the exterior. It can also mean clearing weeps, correcting an irrigation head, or addressing a roof detail two stories up. The interior side is a separate question and it is a moisture question first. Wet material has to be identified before it is covered. Moisture meters and, where appropriate, thermal imaging can map how far the wetting extends beyond the visible stain. Cavity insulation that has been repeatedly wet does not recover its performance and generally comes out. Drywall that has been wet long enough to lose integrity or grow anything comes out with it. Framing that is structurally sound gets dried and verified dry before anything closes over it, because sealing moisture inside a wall is how a small problem becomes a much larger one. Only after that does it become finish work: insulation, drywall, texture matched to the rest of the wall, primer, paint, trim and casing. That sequence, drying and mitigation first, then rebuild, is the same sequence that applies to any interior water damage, and it is worth understanding so you know what to ask about. You can read more about how water damage restoration handles the drying and removal side, and how reconstruction and rebuild handles putting the wall, texture and finishes back once the cavity is dry.

cards.heading: Signs that point to caulk or sealant
cards.body: Leaking only during wind driven rain, visible gap or hardened shrunken caulk at the frame perimeter, stain that appears at the head or upper corner of the window first.

cards.heading: Signs that point to flashing
cards.body: Recurring leak after the joint has already been re-caulked, staining that appears well below or beside the window, stucco cracks radiating from the upper corners, wetting that repeats every storm season.

cards.heading: Signs that point to weeps or the sill
cards.body: Water sitting in the bottom track after rain, swollen baseboard directly under the window, damage concentrated at the sill and lower jambs rather than the head.

cards.heading: Signs that point somewhere else entirely
cards.body: Stain that grows during a storm but the window itself tests dry under a hose, damage at an interior wall near the window, or wetting that appears at the ceiling line above the window head.

sections.heading: There is no urgency to decide today, but there is a reason not to keep painting over it
sections.body: A slow window leak is not an emergency in the way a broken pipe is. Nothing is going to flood tonight. That is genuinely good news, and it means you can take the time to understand the problem rather than react to it. What does change with time is scope. Wet framing and wet sheathing degrade slowly and quietly, and the cost difference between opening a two foot section of wall and rebuilding a wet corner from the sheathing out is significant. Every repaint over an active leak also removes the one signal you had. The stain was doing you a favor. So the practical middle ground is this: document it. Photograph the area, date the photos, note what the weather was doing when it looked worst. Check the weeps and the irrigation, because those are free and they are sometimes the entire answer. If the stain returns after those are ruled out, or if the drywall feels soft, or if you smell that earthy odor near the window, the wall is telling you the water is getting behind the surface and the answer is not on the surface. At that point a look at the cavity is worth more than another guess. faqs.q: My window is foggy between the panes. Does that mean water is getting into my wall?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Fogging or a hazy mineral film between the two panes of glass means the insulated glass unit seal has failed, which is a problem with that glass unit itself. Moisture is trapped inside the sealed cavity, not running into your framing. It affects clarity and insulating performance, and the usual fix is replacing the glass unit or the window. A wet wall is a separate failure, generally at the perimeter caulk, the flashing, or the weep drainage. It is entirely possible to have one without the other, and it is worth checking for both rather than assuming the fog explains the stain.

faqs.q: I re-caulked around the window and it leaked again the next storm. What did I miss?
faqs.a: That is the single most common outcome, and it usually means the caulk was never the real barrier. Behind a properly built window opening there should be flashing, a sill pan and a lapped weather resistive barrier that catch incidental water and drain it back out to the wall surface. If that layer is missing, installed in the wrong lap order, or cut short at the corners, then surface sealant is the only defense and it will keep failing. It can also mean the water is entering somewhere above the window, at a roof to wall junction or an upper opening, and simply surfacing at the window head because that is the first horizontal interruption it hits. Isolating with a hose, one zone at a time, is how you tell the difference.

faqs.q: How much of the wall usually has to come out?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on how far the water traveled and how long it has been happening, which is why moisture mapping comes before demolition rather than after. Water enters high and runs down inside the cavity, so the wet area is normally larger than the stain you see, often extending down to the bottom plate and out past the window jambs. Insulation that has been repeatedly wet generally comes out because it holds moisture and no longer performs. Drywall that has lost integrity or has growth on the back side comes out too. Framing that is still sound gets dried and verified dry before anything is closed back up. The goal is to remove what will not recover and dry what will, not to open more wall than the problem requires.

faqs.q: Is this something my home insurance would cover?
faqs.a: Coverage varies by policy and by carrier, so the honest answer is that you need to read your policy and talk to your adjuster. As a general pattern, insurance often responds to sudden and accidental water events and is much less likely to respond to long term seepage or damage attributed to deferred maintenance, which is a category a slow window leak can fall into. That is one more reason to document the timeline with dated photos as soon as you notice it. Either way, the physical work of drying, removal and rebuild is the same, and it is reasonable to ask any contractor to document conditions and scope clearly so you have something to submit.
